title: Ashwagandha and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Timing, Sedation and Liver Risks
excerpt: Can you drink on ashwagandha? How the herb and alcohol overlap in the brain, the cortisol tug-of-war, how long to wait between them, liver risks, and who should avoid mixing them.
metaDescription: Can you drink on ashwagandha? How it overlaps with alcohol in the brain, how long to wait between them, liver risks, and who should avoid mixing them.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there's no known dangerous interaction between ashwagandha and a drink or two for most healthy adults, but nobody has actually studied the combination in people. What we do know is that both ashwagandha and alcohol can make you drowsy, both appear to act on the same calming system in the brain (the GABA system), and both have been linked to liver problems in some people. So the sensible approach is not panic and not "it's natural, so it's fine." It's to keep drinking light, separate the two in time, skip your bedtime dose on nights you drink, and talk to a doctor if you take any medication that makes you sleepy or affects your thyroid.

**The quick rules:** Take ashwagandha in the morning on days you plan to drink, not right before you go out. Skip any evening or bedtime dose on drinking nights. Expect alcohol to hit a bit harder at first and drink less than you usually would. Never drive after combining them. Don't take extra ashwagandha the next morning to "fix" a hangover, because there's no evidence it works that way. And if you drink heavily on a regular basis, the liver question matters more than the timing question, so check with a doctor before using it at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on ashwagandha and alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before combining ashwagandha and alcohol if** you take benzodiazepines (like Xanax or Valium), prescription sleep aids, opioids, antidepressants, anti-seizure medicines, thyroid medication, immunosuppressants, or medicines for diabetes or blood pressure; if you are pregnant or breastfeeding; if you have liver disease, a thyroid condition, or an autoimmune condition; or if you have a history of alcohol use disorder. **Get medical help right away if** someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or confused after drinking, or if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs while taking ashwagandha. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Ashwagandha Is and Why People Take It

Ashwagandha (*Withania somnifera*) is a shrub whose root has been used in Ayurvedic medicine, the traditional medicine of India, for a very long time. Its species name, *somnifera*, roughly means "sleep-inducing," which is a useful clue for this article. Modern supplements are usually a root extract, sometimes standardized to a group of natural compounds called **withanolides**, which researchers believe are responsible for much of its effect.

It's usually sold as an **adaptogen**, a loose term for herbs said to help the body handle stress. That word isn't a medical category, but the reasons people take ashwagandha are fairly specific:

- **Stress and anxiety.** This is where the human evidence is strongest. Several small randomized trials, including one by Chandrasekhar and colleagues (*Indian Journal of Psychological Medicine*, 2012) and another by Salve and colleagues (*Cureus*, 2019), found lower stress scores in people taking ashwagandha root extract for about two months compared with placebo.
- **Sleep.** Trials have reported modest improvements in how quickly people fall asleep and how well they rate their sleep. A 2021 review and meta-analysis by Cheah and colleagues in *PLoS One* pooled these studies and found a small but real benefit, mainly in people with insomnia and mainly with longer use.
- **Cortisol.** Some of those same stress trials measured morning cortisol, the body's main stress hormone, and found it lower in the ashwagandha groups.

Two things are worth noticing. First, these effects build over **weeks of daily use**, not from a single pill. Second, the studies are mostly small, short, and often funded by companies that sell branded extracts. The evidence is encouraging but not rock solid, and it says nothing directly about alcohol.

## How Ashwagandha and Alcohol Overlap in the Brain

To understand why the combination deserves some care, it helps to know a bit about the brain's brakes.

Your brain balances "go" signals and "slow down" signals. The main slow-down messenger is **GABA**. When GABA attaches to its receptors (called GABA-A receptors), nerve cells become less excitable. That's the feeling of calm, drowsiness, and relaxation. Many sedating drugs work by making these receptors respond more strongly, including benzodiazepines, many sleeping pills, and alcohol.

### Alcohol's side of the overlap

Alcohol boosts GABA-A receptors and at the same time dampens one of the brain's main "go" systems (glutamate, through receptors called NMDA receptors). More brake and less gas is why a few drinks feel relaxing and why too many lead to slurred speech, poor coordination, and eventually dangerous sedation.

### Ashwagandha's side of the overlap

Lab and animal research suggests ashwagandha extracts also interact with GABA receptors. Older rodent work from India described "GABA-like" activity, and later lab studies found that ashwagandha extracts and some of its compounds can act on GABA receptors in cells. This is the most likely explanation for its calming and sleep-promoting effects.

The important caveat: this evidence comes from test tubes and animals, not from people who were drinking. We don't know how strong the GABA effect is at normal supplement doses in humans, and we don't know how it adds up with alcohol. What it does mean is that **both are pushing on the same brake**, and when two things push on the same brake, the sensible assumption is that the effects can add up.

### What that adds up to in real life

For most people taking a standard dose of ashwagandha and having a drink or two, this probably means nothing more than feeling a bit sleepier than usual. The concerns grow when:

- you drink heavily, because alcohol's own sedation becomes the main danger and anything that adds to it matters more;
- you also take a prescription sedative, sleep aid, or opioid, because now three things are pressing on the brake;
- you take ashwagandha at bedtime and drink in the evening, which lines up the peak effects of both;
- you're new to ashwagandha and don't yet know how it affects you.

Feeling extra drowsy isn't just a comfort issue. It can make you underestimate how impaired you are, which matters for driving, for walking home, and for deciding whether to have another drink.

## The Cortisol Angle: Why Alcohol Works Against What Ashwagandha Is For

Most people take ashwagandha to feel less stressed. Alcohol is, for many people, also a way to feel less stressed. The problem is that the two work on very different timelines.

**Alcohol relaxes you now and stresses your body later.** Drinking, especially heavy drinking, raises cortisol. Research going back decades has shown that alcohol activates the body's stress system (the hormone chain running from the brain to the adrenal glands, called the HPA axis), and that regular heavy drinking can leave that system out of balance. As alcohol wears off, the brain's GABA system is left under-stimulated and its glutamate system overactive, which is part of why people feel jittery, anxious, and on edge the next day. That feeling has a popular name: hangxiety. We explain it in detail in our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research).

**Ashwagandha's stress benefits build slowly.** The trials that found lower cortisol and stress scores ran for about 6 to 8 weeks of daily use. The idea is a gradual turning-down of the stress response, not a quick fix.

Put those together and the logic is straightforward. An occasional drink is unlikely to undo weeks of ashwagandha use. But a pattern of regular heavy drinking pushes cortisol and next-day anxiety in exactly the direction you're taking ashwagandha to avoid. If stress is why you take it, cutting back on alcohol will likely do more for that goal than any supplement.

### Can ashwagandha help with anxiety after drinking?

People often ask whether ashwagandha can take the edge off hangover anxiety. Honestly, nobody knows, because it hasn't been tested. A single dose the morning after is unlikely to do much, since its benefits in trials came from weeks of daily use. If you already take it daily for general stress, your baseline anxiety may be a little lower, which could make bad mornings feel less intense, but that is a guess and not a finding.

A small amount of animal research has looked at ashwagandha during alcohol withdrawal in rodents, with some studies reporting less anxiety-like behavior. That's interesting, but rodent withdrawal studies are a long way from a person's Sunday morning, and they are certainly not a reason to use ashwagandha to manage real alcohol withdrawal. **Alcohol withdrawal in a heavy daily drinker can be dangerous and needs medical supervision.**

## How Long After Ashwagandha Can I Drink?

This is the question most people actually search for, so here's a direct answer.

**There is no official waiting period.** No clinical study has measured how long you should wait between ashwagandha and alcohol, and you should be wary of any website that gives you a precise number of hours as if it were established. The compounds in ashwagandha haven't been well mapped in humans in terms of how fast they peak and clear, and products vary a lot in strength.

What we can say is practical rather than precise:

1. **Take it in the morning on drinking days.** If you normally take ashwagandha once a day, moving that dose to the morning puts many hours between it and your first drink in the evening. That's the simplest way to reduce the overlap of peak drowsiness.
2. **Skip your evening or bedtime dose on nights you drink.** Many people take ashwagandha at night for sleep. On a drinking night, that's the dose to drop. Missing one dose won't undo your progress, because its effects build over weeks.
3. **Don't take it right before going out "to stay calm."** Taking it shortly before drinking lines up its sedating effect with the rising alcohol level. That's the timing most likely to leave you more impaired than you expect.
4. **Remember it's never fully "out."** If you take ashwagandha daily, part of its effect comes from steady, ongoing use. Spacing doses lowers the overlap, but it doesn't reset you to zero. That's why drinking less matters as much as timing.

### Ashwagandha and alcohol timing by situation

| Situation | Sensible approach |
|---|---|
| You take ashwagandha every morning | Keep your morning dose, drink moderately, and pay attention to extra drowsiness. |
| You take ashwagandha at bedtime for sleep | Skip the bedtime dose on nights you drink. Resume the next night. |
| You take it twice a day | Take the morning dose, skip the evening dose on drinking nights. |
| You've just started ashwagandha | Wait until you know how it affects you (a week or two) before drinking with it, and start with less alcohol than usual. |
| You also take a sedative, sleep aid, or opioid | Talk to your doctor before combining any of these with alcohol or ashwagandha. |
| You plan to drink heavily | The timing matters less than the amount. Consider skipping ashwagandha that day and seriously reconsider the plan. |

## How Long After Drinking Can I Take Ashwagandha?

The other direction matters too. If you've been drinking, wait until the alcohol is out of your system before your next dose. Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, though this varies a lot with body size, sex, food, and genetics. After a big night, that often means the next morning or later, not when you get home.

The most common mistake is taking a bedtime dose after a night out out of habit. You don't need it. Alcohol is already sedating you (and wrecking the second half of your sleep, as we explain in our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025)). Adding ashwagandha on top doesn't repair alcohol's effect on sleep quality, and it adds to the overall sedation at a time when your judgment is already off.

## Ashwagandha, Alcohol, and Your Liver

This is the part that rarely gets mentioned on supplement websites, and it's the most important one for regular drinkers.

**Ashwagandha has been linked to rare cases of liver injury.** A case series from Iceland and the US published by Björnsson and colleagues in *Liver International* (2020) described people who developed liver injury while taking ashwagandha products, and the US National Institutes of Health's LiverTox database, which tracks drug and supplement liver injury, includes an entry on it. In reported cases, the injury usually showed up within a few weeks to a few months of starting, often with jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) and itching, and most people recovered after stopping. Several European regulators have reviewed ashwagandha's safety in recent years, and Denmark moved to restrict its sale in 2023.

To keep this in proportion: these cases are rare, and millions of people take ashwagandha without liver problems. It's also hard to know which ingredient caused the problem in some cases, because supplements can be mislabeled or contaminated.

**Why this matters more if you drink.** Your liver does most of the work of breaking down alcohol, and heavy drinking is one of the main causes of liver disease. Nobody has shown that alcohol makes ashwagandha liver injury more likely. But if your liver is already under strain from regular drinking, adding another substance with a known (if rare) liver risk is not a great idea, and it may be harder to tell what's causing a problem if one shows up.

**Stop ashwagandha and see a doctor if you notice:**

- yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes;
- dark urine or pale stools;
- itching all over without a rash;
- pain or tenderness under the right ribs;
- unusual tiredness, nausea, or loss of appetite that doesn't go away.

If you drink three or more drinks most days, or you've been told your liver enzymes are high, talk to a doctor before starting ashwagandha. For an overview of what actually supports liver health, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## Other Ashwagandha Interactions That Matter When You Drink

Alcohol is rarely the only thing in the picture. These are the interactions that come up most often:

- **Benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, and opioids.** These are the big ones. They all push on the brake, alcohol pushes on it hard, and ashwagandha may add a little more. Alcohol combined with benzodiazepines or opioids can slow breathing to dangerous levels on its own. Don't add ashwagandha to that mix without a doctor's input, and don't drink on these medications unless your prescriber has said it's okay.
- **Thyroid medication.** Ashwagandha may raise thyroid hormone levels. A small trial by Sharma and colleagues (*Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine*, 2018) found it increased thyroid hormones in people with mildly underactive thyroids. That could matter if you take levothyroxine or have an overactive thyroid. Rare cases of thyroid overactivity have also been reported.
- **Immunosuppressants and autoimmune conditions.** Ashwagandha may stimulate parts of the immune system, which is a concern for people on drugs meant to calm it down.
- **Diabetes and blood pressure medication.** Some studies suggest ashwagandha may lower blood sugar and blood pressure. Alcohol can also lower blood sugar, especially on an empty stomach. If you're on medication for either, the combination is worth discussing with your doctor.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding.** Ashwagandha is generally advised against in pregnancy, and alcohol should be avoided. This one is simple.
- **Surgery.** Because of its sedating effects, it's usually recommended to stop ashwagandha about two weeks before scheduled surgery.

Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how to think about supplement-drug interactions more generally.

## What About Stacking Ashwagandha With DHM or Other "Before Drinking" Supplements?

Many people who take ashwagandha also use other supplements around drinking. A few honest points:

**DHM also appears to act on GABA receptors.** DHM (dihydromyricetin) is the supplement this site focuses on. The best-known study on it, by Shen and colleagues in the *Journal of Neuroscience* (2012), found that in rats DHM reduced alcohol intoxication and appeared to work by counteracting alcohol's effect on GABA-A receptors. That research is promising but comes mostly from animals, and human evidence is limited. Because ashwagandha, DHM, and alcohol all appear to involve the GABA system, no one can tell you exactly how the three behave together. It hasn't been studied.

That doesn't mean you can't use both. It means the same common-sense rules apply: take ashwagandha in the morning, skip the evening dose on drinking nights, keep drinking moderate, and pay attention to how you feel. If you take any prescription medicine, ask first.

**Other calming supplements add up too.** Magnesium (especially glycinate), L-theanine, valerian, kava, melatonin, and GABA supplements all have some sedating effect. Kava in particular has its own liver-safety history and is a poor partner for alcohol. Stacking several calming supplements with ashwagandha and alcohol is the kind of "more is better" thinking that leads to feeling far more impaired than you planned. If you're curious about magnesium specifically, our [magnesium for hangovers and hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/magnesium-hangover-hangxiety-glycinate-vs-citrate-2026) explains which forms make sense and when.

For a broader look at what's worth taking before a night out, and what's a waste of money, see our guide to [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking). And for the basics that matter more than any pill (food, water, pacing, and stopping earlier), our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) is the place to start.

## Ashwagandha, Alcohol, and Sleep

A lot of people take ashwagandha specifically to sleep better, and a lot of people have a drink to wind down at night. It's worth being clear about how these interact.

Alcohol helps you fall asleep faster, but it makes the second half of the night worse. As your body clears it, you get more awakenings, lighter sleep, and less REM sleep (the dreaming stage tied to mood and memory). That's why you can sleep eight hours after drinking and still wake up exhausted.

Ashwagandha's sleep benefit in trials was modest and built up over weeks. Taking it on top of alcohol won't fix alcohol's damage to the second half of the night, because that damage comes from the rebound as alcohol leaves your system. If your goal is better sleep, the evidence points to fewer drinks, finishing your last one a few hours before bed, and keeping ashwagandha (if you use it) for your non-drinking nights. Our guide to [improving sleep quality naturally with GABA and DHM](/never-hungover/sleep-optimization-gaba-dhm-improve-sleep-quality-naturally-2025) goes deeper on sleep habits for people who drink socially.

## Is Ashwagandha Useful for Cutting Back on Drinking?

You may see claims that ashwagandha reduces alcohol cravings. Some rodent studies have looked at this, with mixed and preliminary results, but there are no solid human trials showing it helps people drink less. If you're trying to cut back, the tools with real evidence are behavioral support and, where appropriate, prescription medications that a doctor can discuss with you. If you drink heavily every day, **don't stop suddenly without medical advice**, because alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and can be life-threatening.

## Choosing an Ashwagandha Product If You Do Use It

If you decide ashwagandha is worth taking, a few things reduce risk:

- **Choose root extracts from brands that publish testing.** Look for third-party testing seals (such as USP or NSF) that check for contaminants and confirm what's in the bottle. Supplements aren't approved by the FDA before sale, and quality varies.
- **Stick to studied doses.** Most trials used roughly 250 to 600 mg a day of root extract. Higher doses don't have better evidence and may raise the chance of side effects.
- **Avoid multi-herb "stress" or "sleep" blends** if you drink, because it's harder to know what you're taking and how it adds up with alcohol.
- **Take breaks.** Most trials lasted two to three months. Long-term safety data are thin.
- **Watch for side effects.** The most common are stomach upset, diarrhea, and drowsiness.

## The Bottom Line

- No dangerous interaction between ashwagandha and moderate alcohol has been documented in healthy adults, but the combination has never been properly studied in people.
- Both appear to act on the brain's GABA system and both can make you drowsy, so the main short-term risk is **more sedation and impairment than you expect**.
- **Take ashwagandha in the morning on drinking days, skip the evening dose, and drink less than usual.** There's no official waiting period, and anyone giving you an exact number of hours is guessing.
- Ashwagandha has been linked to rare liver injury, so **regular heavy drinkers and anyone with liver disease should talk to a doctor first**.
- Alcohol pushes cortisol and next-day anxiety in the opposite direction from why most people take ashwagandha. If stress is your goal, drinking less will likely do more than any supplement.
- If you take sedatives, sleep aids, opioids, or thyroid medication, **ask your doctor before mixing any of these with alcohol or ashwagandha.**

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking ashwagandha?**

There's no well-documented dangerous interaction between ashwagandha and a moderate amount of alcohol in healthy adults, but there are also no human studies that tested the combination directly. Both can make you drowsy and both act on the brain's calming (GABA) system, so the main risks are extra sedation, worse judgment about how drunk you are, and added strain on the liver if you drink heavily. Keep drinks light, skip your evening dose on nights you drink, and never drive. If you take sedatives, sleep aids, or thyroid medication, ask your doctor first.

**How long after taking ashwagandha can I drink alcohol?**

No study has set an official waiting period. A practical approach is to take ashwagandha in the morning on days you plan to drink, so several hours pass before your first drink, and to skip any evening or bedtime dose that night. Because ashwagandha is usually taken daily for weeks, some of its effect is always present, so a gap of a few hours lowers the overlap of peak drowsiness but does not make the combination risk-free. Drink less than you normally would until you know how you react.

**How long after drinking can I take ashwagandha?**

Wait until the alcohol has cleared your system before taking your next dose. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people, so after a heavy night that often means waiting until the next morning or later. If you take ashwagandha at bedtime for sleep, skip that dose on nights you've been drinking rather than taking it on top of alcohol.

**Does ashwagandha help with hangovers or hangover anxiety?**

There's no human research showing ashwagandha prevents or treats hangovers. Its best evidence is for daily stress and sleep over several weeks, so a single dose the morning after drinking is unlikely to do much. Some people take it as part of a routine to manage general anxiety, which can make post-drinking anxiety feel less intense, but that's an indirect effect and it hasn't been tested in hangover studies.

**Is ashwagandha bad for your liver if you drink?**

Ashwagandha has been linked to rare cases of liver injury, documented in case reports and in the US National Institutes of Health LiverTox database. Most people who take it have no liver problems, but because alcohol also stresses the liver, people who drink heavily, have liver disease, or have abnormal liver tests should talk to a doctor before using it. Stop taking it and get checked if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching, or pain under the right ribs.

**Does ashwagandha lower cortisol, and does alcohol undo that?**

Several small clinical trials found that people taking ashwagandha daily for about two months had lower morning cortisol and lower stress scores than people taking a placebo. Alcohol pushes the other way: heavy drinking raises cortisol and disrupts the body's stress system, and the rebound as alcohol wears off contributes to next-day anxiety. A few drinks won't erase weeks of supplement use, but regular heavy drinking works directly against the reason most people take ashwagandha.

**Can I take ashwagandha and DHM together when drinking?**

No study has tested ashwagandha, DHM, and alcohol together. Both supplements appear to interact with the brain's GABA system in lab research, and alcohol does too, so stacking all three is a reason to be cautious about drowsiness. If you want to use DHM on a night out, a sensible approach is to take ashwagandha in the morning, skip the evening dose, keep drinking moderate, and check with a doctor if you take any prescription medication. Popular DHM options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20).

**Who should not mix ashwagandha and alcohol?**

Avoid the combination, or ask a doctor first, if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, take benzodiazepines, sleep medications, opioids, or other sedatives, take thyroid medication or have a thyroid condition, have liver disease, take immunosuppressants, take medication for diabetes or blood pressure, or have a history of alcohol use disorder. Ashwagandha should also be stopped before scheduled surgery because of its sedating effects.
